You are Sunny's Experience Creator. Build one complete child-facing activity as self-contained HTML with inline CSS and JavaScript.

Creative objective:
Build an experience a child would voluntarily replay. The mathematics must be the power the child uses to affect the world, not an unrelated question interrupting play. The child's meaningful action must visibly transform the world, mission, progression, or payoff. Choose the interaction, stakes, consequences, pacing, and reward that best serve the Planner's prescription and the factual evidence. Commit to one distinctive core interaction whose first action is understandable from the finished screen.

The AI Planner already made the educational decision below. Implement it faithfully without changing the theory, evidence limit, or purpose:
Build a five-round dock loading run for a 9-year-old. A fixed pod count must be dragged into a rectangle that exactly fits each arriving boat's hold — no gaps, no leftovers, no stacking outside the outline. Round 1: 24 pods, hold is 3 wide, so the child must find 3 × 8. Round 2: same 24 pods, hold is 12 wide, forcing a second decomposition of a product they already 'solved'. Round 3: 36 pods and the boat announces only its depth (4 rows) — the child must work out the width, an unknown-factor solve where the unknown is the group count. Round 4: 14 pods and the harbourmaster asks for a hold that is 4 wide; it genuinely cannot be done, and the child must say so and pick a legal hold instead — this is the direct probe of whether 'a product has one shape' has become 'a product has whichever shapes divide it'. Round 5: an unseen story — 'the lantern barge takes rows of 5 and it must be at least 6 rows deep; load 40 lanterns' — read the constraint, build 5 × 8, and defend why 8 rows and not 4. Between rounds a boat horn sounds and the tide gauge drops one notch. Speak plainly, no baby talk, no confetti for merely finishing a drag. Assignment: Festival Team Challenge. Academic construct to preserve: Lab Learner reliably transfers equal-groups, missing-factor, and word-problem interpretation on practiced material, but holds a uniqueness misconception: a product is treated as having a single valid group structure. Prediction: on unseen composite products Lab Learner will build the first correct rectangle quickly and then stall or repeat it when a different arrangement is demanded, and will attempt an impossible arrangement rather than declare it impossible. This node must test unseen transfer: change the context while preserving the construct. Author fresh items. These have already been seen and must not be reused verbatim: math.multiplication.equal_groups, math.multiplication.missing_factor, math.multiplication.word_problem_interpretation, math.multiplication.factor_pairs. Planner decision behind this node: Baseline accuracy was 0.75, inside the preregistered 0.70–1.00 band, and all four readings were unassisted — but every item was previously_practiced with provenance 'practice', so this supports the transfer hypothesis only as a warrant to test it, never as proof. The single miss landed exactly on the predicted error pattern: on math.multiplication.factor_pairs Lab Learner answered 'only one pair', treating a product as having a unique decomposition. That is a scoped misconception, not a collapse of multiplicative reasoning, so the hypothesis is revised rather than falsified: equal-groups, missing-factor, and word-problem reasoning hold, while the belief that a product names one and only one group-structure does not. Quest eligibility is already met (4 target-aligned, 3 independent correct), so the right move is an unseen-transfer Quest built so that the uniqueness belief is the thing that fails first and visibly. Created at: 2026-08-08T16:13:56.012Z.

Approved design artifact is the creative authority for presentation and interaction. Implement it faithfully; it cannot change the Planner's academic contract.
The first action, core interaction, mathematics-as-power, visible consequences, progression, world reaction, and payoff must exist as child-visible mechanics. Do not collapse the artifact into answer buttons, a question card, decorative artwork, or a progress bar.

  "nodeId": "quest",
  "academicContractHash": "879f3f5fc37bcf3dc51d2cbcc69d0c557033ac533d4c4ed64c50a3e6b05b4a4d",
  "title": "The Shape-Shifting Crate",
  "audienceRationale": "A 9-year-old third-grader with demonstrated unassisted competence on practiced equal-groups, missing-factor, and word-problem items needs a world that respects that competence: plain harbourmaster speech, no baby talk, no tutorial screens — the first drag teaches everything. The evidence hints (uncertain, small-sample) that construction-style activities were replayed and rated highly while a speed-pressured activity was abandoned; this design leans construction-first and keeps time pressure narrative (tide between rounds) rather than reflexive, without copying any prior game. Difficulty deepens along the exact construct sequence the Planner prescribed, so the child is always working one honest step past what practice proved.",
  "openingPromise": "You are the dock loader for the Festival Fleet. Five boats are coming in on a falling tide, and each boat's hold is a different shape. The same pods have to fit every hold exactly — no gaps, no leftovers — or the boat can't sail. If you load all five before the tide gauge empties, the festival lanterns light tonight.",
  "firstThreeSeconds": "The screen opens already alive: a wooden dock in warm evening light, water lapping, a boat gliding in with its hold outlined as a glowing rectangle 3 cells wide. A pallet of 24 pods sits at the child's hand, one pod pulsing gently under the cursor. No menu, no instruction screen. As the boat docks, one plain line appears: \"24 pods. Hold is 3 wide. Fill it exactly.\"",
  "firstAction": "Drag one pod from the pallet into the glowing hold outline. It snaps to the grid with a clunk and the hold's depth counter ticks. The child immediately discovers the core verb — drag pods into a width-constrained rectangle — and discovers the drag-a-whole-row shortcut when they grab the pallet's row handle (a plank that scoops 3 pods at once when the hold is 3 wide).",
  "interactionDemonstration": "Concrete walkthrough of Round 2, the pivotal beat: the Wide Ferry docks; its hold outline is 12 cells across and 2 deep. The same 24 pods sit on the pallet, still faintly ghosted in their old 3 × 8 arrangement. The child grabs the row handle — it now scoops 12 pods at once because the scoop always matches hold width. First scoop lays a full 12-row; the edge-equation writes '12 × 1 = 12... need 24.' Second scoop completes 12 × 2 = 24; both rows lock, the hull eases level, the horn sounds, and the harbourmaster's slate reads: 'Same 24. Different boat, different shape.' If the child instead tries to lay pods 3-across in a corner, the remaining 9 cells of that row stay hollow and the boat lists — the world itself demonstrates that the old shape does not fit the new constraint.",
  "coreInteraction": "Grid-snapped drag-and-drop rectangle construction under constraint. Each round, a fixed pod count must be arranged into a rectangle that exactly fills a boat's hold. The hold fixes one dimension (width, or in Round 3 only the depth, or in Round 5 a story constraint) and the child controls the other by how they load. Pods can be dragged singly or scooped by rows. The hold live-renders the current arrangement as a growing rectangle: complete rows lock and turn solid; a running equation builds along the hold's edge (e.g., \"3 wide × 5 rows = 15 so far... need 24\"). Overfilling a row is physically impossible — pods bounce off the hull with a thud. Leftover pods on the dock when the child hits the LOAD lever cause the boat to list visibly to one side and refuse to sail; a perfect fill makes the hull settle level with a deep horn blast and the boat departs. Round 4 adds a second verb: a red \"CAN'T BE DONE\" flag the child can raise instead of loading, then a hold-width dial to propose a legal width. Round 5 adds a defend step: after loading, the harbourmaster asks \"Why 8 rows and not 4?\" and the child answers by tapping the constraint plaque (\"at least 6 rows deep\") — the arithmetic and the constraint must both be invoked to launch the barge.",
  "mathAsPower": "Multiplication is the loading physics of the world, not a quiz layered on top. The rectangle IS the product: width × rows = pods, drawn cell by cell by the child's own hands. When the child reasons \"24 with 3 across means 8 rows,\" the boat's hold literally extends to 8 rows and the hull sits level — correct factoring makes the boat sailable. When they reason wrongly, the world shows it physically: a 12-wide hold half-filled leaves the boat lopsided in the water; 14 pods forced into 4 columns leaves 2 pods that cannot dock anywhere, rolling on the deck. The missing-factor round makes the unknown tangible: the hold shows 4 fixed rows and an unlit width, and each column the child commits lights another lamp until 4 × ? = 36 resolves as 9 lamps burning. The uniqueness misconception is confronted by the world itself: the SAME 24 pods that made a 3 × 8 boat sail must be reshaped into 12 × 2 for the next boat — the child watches one product wear two shapes, and in Round 4 discovers that a product refuses shapes that don't divide it. Every equation on screen is generated by the child's physical arrangement, never the other way around.",
  "stakes": "The tide is falling. A tide gauge on the dock piling drops one notch after every boat (as prescribed), and the water line visibly recedes down the pilings, barnacles emerging. If the tide runs out before all five boats load, the last boats ground on the mud and the festival opens with dark lanterns. Each boat also has its own patience: a lopsided launch attempt costs a short re-trim delay while the boat rights itself. Nothing punishes thinking time within a round — the tide only moves between boats — so the pressure is narrative and consequential, not a twitch timer (the child's evidence suggests speed-pressure formats have gone badly before, and the contract's construct needs deliberate reasoning to surface).",
  "consequences": "Wrong arrangements have physical, legible consequences: leftover pods roll audibly on the deck and the boat lists toward its loaded side, refusing to sail; an over-wide attempt leaves visible empty cells that flash the shortfall ('12 wide × 1 row = 12... you have 24'). In Round 4, persisting with the impossible 4-wide load leads to the boat listing three times, after which the harbourmaster points silently at the red flag — the world escalates toward the correct concept rather than toward failure. A grounded boat (tide expiry) is a real end-state: the run finishes with a partial festival and the score reflects boats launched, never a fake win.",
  "recovery": "Recovery is always in-world and never resets progress. Pods drag back out of the hold as freely as they went in; the edge-equation recomputes live, so any misstep is one drag from repair. After a failed launch, the harbourmaster gives one concrete, plain-spoken nudge tied to the arithmetic, escalating over attempts: first the numbers ('3 wide. You have 24. How many rows is that?'), then the structure ('Every full row uses 3. Count by 3s until you hit 24.'). In Round 4 the nudge redirects to the flag concept, never to a fake solution. Hints cost nothing academically but are logged as assisted evidence. A grounded run offers immediate 'next tide' replay starting at the failed boat, keeping earlier launches earned.",
  "progression": [
    "Round 1 — The Grain Skiff: 24 pods, hold announced as 3 wide. Child builds 3 × 8. Expected to be fast (practiced-adjacent territory in a new skin). Success: hull settles level, deep horn, boat sails, tide gauge drops one notch. The running edge-equation teaches the notation without a tutorial.",
    "Round 2 — The Wide Ferry: the SAME 24 pods return on the pallet, but this hold is 12 wide. This is the misconception's first collision: the child who believes 24 'is' 3 × 8 must produce 12 × 2. The pallet even briefly shows the ghost of the old 3 × 8 shape dissolving as the new boat docks — the world announces that the pods remember nothing, only the count matters. Success line from the harbourmaster: 'Same 24. Different boat, different shape. Good — pods don't care what shape they wore yesterday.'",
    "Round 3 — The Deep Trawler (missing factor): 36 pods, and the boat announces only its depth: 4 rows, width unlit. The unknown is the group count. Child can probe by committing columns; each committed column of 4 lights a lamp. Solving 4 × ? = 36 lights the 9th lamp and the hold outline snaps shut around exactly 36. Committing a 10th column is impossible — no pods remain — making overshoot self-evident.",
    "Round 4 — The Stubborn Cutter (impossibility probe): 14 pods, harbourmaster demands a hold 4 wide. It cannot be done. Child who attempts it ends with 2 pods rolling loose and a lopsided boat that will not sail no matter what. The correct move is raising the red CAN'T BE DONE flag, then turning the hold-width dial to a legal width (1, 2, 7, or 14) and loading that instead. This is the direct falsification test of 'a product has one shape' becoming 'a product has whichever shapes divide it — and only those.' The harbourmaster respects the flag: 'Right call. 4 doesn't go into 14. Pick a width that does.'",
    "Round 5 — The Lantern Barge (unseen story + constrained defense): a written order arrives: 'The lantern barge takes rows of 5, and it must ride at least 6 rows deep. Load all 40 lanterns.' Child must read the constraint, reject the tempting shallow 4-row option, build 5 × 8, then defend it: harbourmaster asks 'Why 8 rows and not 4?' and the child taps the constraint plaque ('at least 6 rows deep') to justify. On launch, all five boats reconvene offshore and the lanterns light in a 5 × 8 constellation reflected on the water."
  ],
  "interactionContinuity": "One verb carries the whole run — drag pods into a constrained hold — and every round deepens it rather than replacing it. Round 2 reuses the identical pods and verb against a new constraint; Round 3 inverts which dimension is known but the hands do the same work; Round 4 adds the flag and dial as an escalation of the same loading judgment (deciding a load is impossible is still a loading decision); Round 5 adds reading and defending but the build is still the same drag-to-grid act. Nothing learned in Round 1 is ever discarded; each mechanic added is a mathematical idea made manipulable.",
  "worldReaction": "The world reacts to arithmetic truth, never to button presses: the hull's list angle is a continuous function of load imbalance; the edge-equation rewrites on every pod moved; lamps light per committed column in the missing-factor round; the tide line recedes across the entire scene between boats; the red flag, when correctly raised on an impossible order, is answered by the harbourmaster striking the order through on the slate — the demand itself visibly dies. The finale's lantern constellation is rendered from the child's actual final arrangement, so the closing image is their own mathematics made into light.",
  "payoff": "Launching each boat gives a proportionate, earned beat: level hull, horn, wake, tide-gauge notch — no confetti for merely finishing a drag, exactly as prescribed. The full-run payoff is the Festival Launch: all five boats anchor offshore at dusk and the 40 lanterns ignite in the child's own 5 × 8 arrangement, reflected doubled in the water — a final image that literally displays the last product they built. The harbourmaster's closing line names the real achievement in plain words: 'Five boats, five shapes, one loader. You proved a number can wear every shape that fits it — and you knew when one didn't.'",
  "replayVariation": "On replay ('next tide'), the run keeps its five-beat structure but regenerates the arithmetic within the same construct map: Round 1–2 use a fresh composite (e.g., 30 pods at 5 wide, then the same 30 at 6 wide), Round 3 draws a new missing-factor pair (e.g., 3 rows announced, 27 pods), Round 4 draws a new genuinely-impossible demand (e.g., 22 pods, 5 wide), and Round 5 authors a new one-sentence order with a fresh inequality constraint (e.g., 'rows of 6, no more than 7 rows deep, 42 crates'). Boat designs, harbourmaster lines, and weather vary so the world feels new while the tested constructs stay identical. Verbatim baseline items are never reused.",
  "visualDirection": "Warm late-afternoon harbour palette: teak dock planks, deep teal water with animated specular ripples, cream sails, brass fittings. The hold grid is the visual hero — a crisp glowing outline with cells that fill as satisfying solid tiles, complete rows locking with a subtle color shift so the rectangle's structure reads at a glance from across the room. The running edge-equation is set in large, honest numerals along the hold rim, styled as chalk on a loading slate. Pods are chunky, tactile hex-latched crates with slight physical wobble on drag. UI chrome is minimal: pallet, hold, LOAD lever, tide gauge, and (Round 4+) the red flag and width dial — every control is a dock object, not a button bar. Character art (harbourmaster) is a small silhouette with a speech slate; no cartoon mugging. Rendered in clean flat-shaded 2D with parallax water layers.",
  "motionDirection": "Motion is physical and weight-honest: pods arc slightly on drag and snap to cells with a short settle bounce; completed rows lock with a 120ms press-down; the boat's hull responds continuously to load distribution (list angle interpolates with load imbalance, easing level on a perfect fill). Boats glide in on slow ease-in-out with bow wake; departure is a long ease-out with expanding wake rings. The tide-gauge drop is a deliberate 700ms slide with the water line receding across the whole scene. Rejected drops use a firm 80ms bounce-back, never a punitive shake. All feedback lands within 150ms of input; nothing blocks the next drag.",
  "soundDirection": "Ambient bed: low harbour wash, gulls sparse and distant, rope creak. Each pod snap is a wooden clunk pitched up slightly per cell across a row, so a completed row resolves as a small ascending phrase — the arithmetic becomes audible rhythm (rows of 3 sound different from rows of 12). Row lock: soft timber thud. Perfect fill: hull settle groan then the deep boat horn (the prescribed between-round horn), each boat's horn a different low pitch. Lopsided launch attempt: hollow roll of loose pods and a flat, unresolved chord. Round 4 flag raise: single clean bell — the sound of a right call, distinct from the launch horn. Finale: lanterns ignite with soft paper-flame whispers over a quiet swell. No voiceover baby talk; harbourmaster text lines land with a chalk-tap tick.",
  "usefulLibraries": [
    "PixiJS (2D WebGL rendering for water, parallax, and grid tiles)",
    "GSAP (drag snapping, hull-list interpolation, tide and launch easing)",
    "Howler.js (layered ambient bed, pitched pod-snap sequencing, horn/bell cues)",
    "@use-gesture or interact.js (robust touch + mouse drag with grid snap on tablets)"
  ],
  "engagementPrediction": "Rounds 1 and 3 will feel fast and empowering (practiced constructs in a new skin), building investment before the two designed friction points. Round 2 is the first productive struggle: expect a pause, an attempt to rebuild 3 × 8 inside a 12-wide hold, then a visible reorganization insight when the ghost-shape dissolve lands. Round 4 is the emotional peak — the first game moment where 'refuse the task' is the winning move — predicted to produce either a triumphant flag raise or up to three listing attempts before the concept clicks. Round 5's defend step converts relief into articulated understanding. Predicted session: 8–14 minutes, high completion drive from the fleet-assembly finale, and replay appetite driven by the 'next tide' variation rather than score chasing.",
  "falsifyingEvidence": "The design's academic bet fails if: (a) in Round 2 the child produces 12 × 2 immediately and without hesitation, and in Round 4 raises the flag on the first look — indicating the uniqueness misconception was already resolved and this Quest under-challenges; or (b) in Round 2 the child stalls terminally (3+ failed launches even after both nudges) and in Round 4 never raises the flag despite the escalating point-at-flag prompt — indicating the misconception is deeper than 'scoped' and the transfer hypothesis itself is wrong, not merely untested. Engagement-side falsifiers: abandonment during the tide-gauge drop (pressure misread as a timer), or the child launching boats by trial-and-error pod dumping without ever reading the edge-equation (the world's math channel failed to carry meaning). Each of these is observable in the evidence stream: launch-attempt counts, flag latency, hint escalation depth, and drag-pattern entropy per round."
}


The Planner's design decisions for this node. Build these; do not soften them:
- Core interaction: The child drags glowing pods from a loose pile at the bottom of the screen into a rectangular hold outline at the top. Pods snap to a grid inside the outline. A live readout under the hold reads 'rows × per row = loaded' and updates on every drop, so 3 rows of 7 shows '3 × 7 = 21' with 3 pods still glowing on the dock. Grabbing the corner handle of an already-built block reshapes it — pull it wide and the rows recompute, and pods that no longer fit pop back out to the dock, visibly. Pressing SAIL locks the layout: if it exactly fills the hold, the outline seals and the boat pulls away with a horn. If it doesn't, the hold flashes red at the empty cells or the overflow pods, the tide gauge drops a notch, and the boat waits. Failure on screen is loose pods dimming to grey on an empty dock as the boat's lights recede upriver.
- What is at risk: The tide is going out. A gauge on the pier drops one notch every 45 seconds and every time the child submits a layout that doesn't exactly fill the hold. When the gauge hits bottom the boat leaves on the tide with whatever fitted, and the pods still loose on the dock stay behind — the child watches them go dark one by one, and the dock counter shows how many pods missed the sailing. Those pods are gone from the run; the final tally at the end of the night is the pods that sailed, not a score out of five. A child who finds only the first arrangement they already know will strand cargo in round 2 and feel exactly why one factor pair is not enough.
- How a run goes wrong: A run ends badly when the tide runs out with pods still on the dock. Concretely: the child rebuilds the same familiar rectangle for a hold it cannot fit, or keeps nudging pods without changing the row count, and the gauge empties. The boat sails, the stranded pods go dark, and that count carries into the final tally — it cannot be recovered by doing well later. Round 4 has its own failure: forcing a 4-wide layout onto 14 pods leaves two pods hanging outside the outline every single time, and burning the tide trying is the cost of not accepting that some widths simply don't divide.
- How pressure builds: Round 1 gives a product Lab Learner has met and a width that quietly forbids the memorized arrangement. Round 2 returns to that same product to demand a different shape — the first real jolt. Round 3 removes the width entirely so the factor must be reasoned, not seen. Round 4 removes the guarantee of success and asks for a judgment about impossibility. Round 5 removes the numbers from view altogether and hides them inside a sentence with a constraint, with the tide already lower because the earlier rounds cost time. Tide drain rate increases slightly each round.
- The mathematical hook to make visible: The same 24 pods are a 4-by-6 block, a 3-by-8 block, a 2-by-12 block, and a 1-by-24 line — the pile never changes, only the shape does. A number is not one arrangement; it carries a whole family of them, and it is your job to know which ones it owns. And then 14 arrives and flatly refuses to become 4 rows, no matter how you push — which is the moment a child feels that numbers have shapes they can have and shapes they can't, and that this is a fact about the number, not about how hard you try.
If the Planner specified a way to fail, that failure must be genuinely reachable on screen and must cost the child something they can see. Do not replace it with a hint, a retry, or an encouraging message.

Never display the answer to a question before the child has committed to a response.

Author fresh content appropriate to this assignment and node responsibility. Do not reuse any exposed item identity or exact prompt listed in the cycle. Quest must test unseen transfer. Boss must test unseen synthesis. A generated support node remains teaching/practice evidence. Do not claim mastery.
The first visible H1 must be exactly "The Shape-Shifting Crate". A short exciting subtitle may establish the AI-authored world.
Visibly use the assigned artwork URL as part of the world: none.
Keep the complete HTML under 24,000 characters. Prefer concise CSS and JavaScript.
Every DOM element queried by JavaScript must exist before the query runs; place behavior after its markup or initialize it on DOMContentLoaded.

Runtime contract appendix:
Load <script src="/games/_contract.js"></script> in <head>.
Read runtime identity and parameters from window.GAME_PARAMS. Never hardcode the child identity, homework identity, or session identity into the HTML.
Emit window.parent.postMessage({type:"activity_ready",payload:{nodeId:"quest"}},"*") when ready.
Whenever the activity or problem changes, emit window.parent.postMessage({type:"game_state_update",payload:{game:"generated-math",activityId:"quest",nodeId:"quest",phase:"question",activityTitle:"The Shape-Shifting Crate",learningFocus:"math.multiplication.transfer — producing multiple valid factor pairs for one product, and solving for an unknown factor under a stated constraint, in unseen contexts",mechanic:"Drag-to-rearrange packing puzzle: the same fixed pile of cargo must be rebuilt into different rectangular crate layouts on demand, with a shipping clock running.",currentChallenge,availableActions,itemIndex,totalItems,answerVisibility:"hidden"}},"*") so Elli has live context. Never expose answers.
Represent currentChallenge as {id,prompt,mode,readAloudRequested:false,readAloudCount}. When the child activates a visible Read it to me control, increment readAloudCount and resend that same answer-hidden state with readAloudRequested:true. Do not narrate it inside the activity.
Listen for parent messages with type:"sunny_companion_presence". Pause activity timers and input while summoned, and resume the same state when collapsed. Do not restart or change progress.
Maintain a factual targetResults array. For every submitted answer append {target,correct,attemptedValue,responseTimeMs,scaffoldLevel} using a stable fresh item identity.
For every answer call window.fireAttemptEvent({domain:"math",target,correct,attemptedValue,responseTimeMs,scaffoldLevel}).
Emit window.parent.postMessage({type:"progress_event",payload:{nodeId:"quest",completedItems,totalItems}},"*") whenever visible progress advances.
Use window.fireCompanionEvent("correct_answer" or "wrong_answer", {target}) after meaningful answers and window.fireCompanionEvent("game_complete", {}) at completion.
On completion calculate accuracy from targetResults and call window.sendNodeComplete({nodeId:window.GAME_PARAMS.nodeId,completed:true,accuracy,targetResults,timeSpent_ms}).
Expose window.SUNNY_VALIDATION_HOOKS = {playthrough: async () => { ... }}. This is required for Quest and Boss. The hook must use the same handlers as visible child controls, exercise an incorrect response and visible recovery, complete every assessable item, and reach completion. It must not fabricate or post evidence directly.
Include <div id="sunny-companion"></div>; Sunny owns its rendering, so do not create companion chrome. Return raw HTML only and end with </html>.
